model.step: Apply the governing principle: Kling 3.0 when the shot is built around a face, Seedance 2.0 when the shot is built around movement or scale.
Assign close-up shots requiring realistic facial expression and emotion to Kling 3.0.
Assign emotional dialogue delivery with natural voice performance to Kling 3.0.
Assign tight product detail shots where label and texture accuracy matter to Kling 3.0.
Assign intimate, character-driven moments where the face is the subject to Kling 3.0.
Assign action sequences — running, jumping, physical confrontations, dynamic movement — to Seedance 2.0.
Assign wide shots and medium shots with multiple characters in motion to Seedance 2.0.
Assign environmental scale shots — buildings, crowds, large spaces — to Seedance 2.0.
Assign clips requiring strict multimodal reference consistency across the full scene to Seedance 2.0.
For videos needing both models, split the generations so close-up and dialogue beats go to Kling and wider action-driven beats go to Seedance, planning to cut both sets together in post.
Never mix Kling and Seedance rule sets — Seedance is zero-memory per prompt, Kling shares context across shot boxes within one generation.
Treat Kling as zero-memory BETWEEN generations — every new Kling generation needs its own full Shot Box 1 global setup.
Verify every Kling generation in the plan fits inside the hard 15-second cap and state its estimated duration in the plan.
Split any Kling generation that would run past 15 seconds at a natural break point, giving each new generation its own full Shot Box 1 setup and its own start frame or references.
Present the shot plan as a numbered list of generations stating model and mode, shots or dialogue lines covered, a one-sentence reason, the reference images needed, and the estimated duration.
Write no prompt of any kind until the operator has approved the plan.
For every generation already assigned to Kling, ask the default question: is this scene super simple?

Route to Kling 3.0 General only when ALL three are true: the shots are simple static dialogue lines delivered to or near camera; the head is not turning much so consistency holds from the start frame alone; the generation is a single angle or a batch of same-angle dialogue lines.

Route to Kling 3.0 Omni when ANY one is true: the generation needs multiple references at once (character sheet plus scene stills plus product); it covers multiple camera angles or multiple characters in one multi-shot sequence; the character turns their head significantly, shows front and side views, or moves through the scene.

Reject any routing of a super simple dialogue scene to Omni justified only by Omni being the multi-reference mode — General avoids artifacts better, especially when Omni is overloaded with references.
Show the operator guide/images/kling-3-omni-multi-reference-images-compared-to-kling-3-0-ge.webp when explaining the Omni-versus-General choice.

For dialogue scenes on Kling General, batch ALL of Speaker A's lines in one generation off Speaker A's close-up start frame, and ALL of Speaker B's lines in a second generation off Speaker B's close-up start frame.

Define every character, location, product, and screen reference upfront by name before writing any prompts, in the form "[Name] = @".

Before writing each prompt, go through the script and list every single character that appears in that specific clip, including anyone appearing only briefly in the background.
Double-check each clip's character list before writing the prompt.
Include in each clip's header only what is actually present and visible in that clip — no character, product, screen, or reference that does not appear.
Never describe a character physically in a Seedance prompt — no skin tone, hair color, outfit, or physical detail of any kind; just name and @.
Open every Seedance prompt with the line "Main Subjects:" followed by one bullet per character in the exact form "• [Character name] face and outfit 100% matched based exactly on @".
Repeat any special costume or appearance rules in every single prompt without exception.
Add object lines in the exact form "[Object/asset name] 100% matched based exactly on @" only when the object appears in that clip.
Add screen lines in the exact form "[Screen name] display content 100% matched based exactly on @" only when a screen appears in that clip.

When a location or scene reference image exists for the clip, add the line "Scene setting is based on @" and write zero environment description anywhere in the prompt — no ceiling, floor, wall color, furniture, or lighting fixtures.
When no location image exists for the clip, omit the scene @ line entirely and write a short one-or-two-line setting, location, and time-of-day description in the header instead.
Never do both at once — each clip gets either a scene @ with no environment text, or no scene @ with a written setting description.

Decide whether the clip needs header expression lines to hold or contrast an expression across the whole clip, e.g. "Expression of [side character] is scared" and "[Main character] facial expression remains calm and cold throughout. No panic, no fear."
Paste the selected visual tone string word for word as the "Visual tone:" line of every Seedance prompt.
Add the "Camera feel:" line using the exact library string, Handheld Shaky Camera or Static Shot, per the camera feel answer.
Include the mandatory line "NO MUSIC, only natural ambient sounds." in every single prompt, because Seedance otherwise bakes a music track into the audio that can never be separated out.
Include the mandatory line "No texts or subtitles on screen." in every single prompt, because burnt-in captions cannot be removed once rendered into frames.

Verify the header follows the mandated order: Main Subjects, character lines, costume rules, object lines, screen lines, scene line, expression lines, Visual tone, Camera feel, NO MUSIC, No texts or subtitles, SHOTS.
Write every timecode in plain seconds with a dash, using decimals for half seconds: 0-1.5s, 1.5-3s, 3-4.5s, 4.5-7s.
Never use clock formats like 00:04:30 or 00:00–00:02, or minute:second:frame notation of any kind.
Count the total dialogue words for a prompt and match them to the duration scale (4s = 9-12 words up to 15s = 35-45 words) before writing the prompt.
Never assign a duration longer than the word count supports, and never pad shots or stretch timecodes to hit a target runtime.
Run the padding test: divide total dialogue words by 35, multiply by 15, and trim the generation if its written duration exceeds that number.
For every shot, first ask whether it contains dialogue; apply the word-count scale plus the selected pacing's breathing room if yes, or the selected pacing's action-shot duration if no.

Apply the chosen pacing profile — fast: no breathing room and 1-3s action shots; medium: plus 1-2s per dialogue shot, 2-4s action shots, 3-5s end card holds; slow: plus 2-4s per dialogue shot, 4-8s action shots, 5-8s end card holds.
Keep each prompt block between 4 and 15 seconds total, and never apply the 4-second block minimum to an individual shot, which may be as short as 0.5 seconds.
Never split a generation at an unnatural point just to hit a round number of seconds.
Use an exact CAMERA LANGUAGE LIBRARY string for every shot's size, angle, view, or blocking in the shot list.
Change the camera angle on every consecutive timecoded shot; the same angle may only return with at least one different angle between the two uses.
State any camera movement with the exact library string — Camera Pushes In, Camera Pulls Back, Camera Pans Right, Circles to the Left — never expecting the model to guess the move.
Vary shot timing naturally to match the energy of each moment — some beats 1s, some 1.5s, some 3s, some 5 or 6s — with quick action beats short and slow emotional beats 4-6s.
Read each shot line out loud and confirm the action can genuinely happen in the time it was given; shorten the action or extend the beat if not.
Tag every reference with its blank @ directly after its name in each shot line where it is visibly on screen; use the name alone with no @ when it is only mentioned or heard.
Specify exactly where each character is positioned in every prompt.
Write dialogue as a character action inside the shot description — "Sarah @ mutters to herself:", "James @ sighs and says out loud:" — never as a voiceover and never labeled "DIALOGUE:".
Make it explicitly clear the character is speaking on screen, not narrating.
Specify how the voice sounds for any special voice condition, e.g. "Astronaut @ says through helmet in muffled futuristic voice:".

Spell out every symbol, abbreviation, sign, and shorthand in dialogue as a full spoken word in both Kling and Seedance prompts: dollars not $, percent not %, fifty thousand not 50K, two million not 2M, and not &, number not #, at not @, plus not +, versus not vs, approximately not approx.
Note that @ reference tags in shot lines are not dialogue — the spell-it-out rule applies only to words inside quotation marks.
For a physical product, have the character physically handle, hold, use, examine, or demonstrate it on screen; never leave it sitting in the background with no interaction.
For software or digital products, always show the UI on a device and have the character interact with the screen; never let a character talk about software without showing it.
Write every screen shot line as "[device] screen displaying the [Screen name] @ as defined in the header, visible and legible on screen", always stating the screen is clearly visible and legible.

If the operator chose green screen placeholders, describe every un-referenced screen as a solid bright green placeholder with five white crosses — one in each of the four corners and one in the exact center — and never omit the crosses.
Include a logo only if the operator explicitly confirmed one via the logo question, and never invent, describe, or place a logo that was not confirmed.
Never reference any TV show, film, brand, or existing IP anywhere in any prompt in any stage.
Wrap every completed prompt in a triple-backtick code block — one Seedance prompt or one Kling shot box per block, never plain text, never two in one block.
If the user confirms they want B-roll, apply these rules across all Seedance prompts:
A-roll and B-roll can be mixed within the same generation prompt.
You do not need a separate prompt for B-roll.
Within a single prompt you can cut between the speaker on camera (A-roll) and cutaway visuals (B-roll) shot by shot, exactly like a real edit.
A-ROLL shots are shots of the main speaker or character on camera, speaking directly or performing an action central to the narrative.
B-ROLL shots are cutaway visuals that support, illustrate or complement what the speaker is saying.
B-roll shots never include the main speaker talking to camera.
Close ups of objects, products, hands, screens, or details being referenced
Environment shots showing a relevant location or setting
Action shots of relevant activities
Atmospheric or mood shots that support the tone of the moment
Text or screen content being referenced
WHEN MIXING A-ROLL AND B-ROLL IN A SINGLE PROMPT follow these rules:
The global header must still include every character and reference that appears in any shot within that prompt, whether A-roll or B-roll
Clearly label each shot as either A-ROLL or B-ROLL within the shot line itself so it is always explicit
B-ROLL shots must still follow all shot rules: exact library camera prompts, camera movement, the angle variation rule, and natural timing variation
B-ROLL shots must never contradict or be visually unrelated to what the speaker is saying in the surrounding A-roll
If B-roll features a product or screen that appears elsewhere in the prompt, it must already be defined in the header with its @, and it gets its @ again in the shot line where it appears
If the user says no to B-roll, write all prompts as pure A-roll talking head shots with varied angles and natural shot movement
DOCUMENTARY A-ROLL AND B-ROLL DIALOGUE RULE — NO EXCEPTIONS
In documentary style videos, the subject is always talking.
Every single shot in the entire prompt — whether A-ROLL or B-ROLL — must have dialogue happening.
There is no shot in a documentary prompt where the subject's voice is not heard.
On A-ROLL shots, the subject speaks directly on camera as normal.
Write it as: "Maria @ says directly to camera: "dialogue here""
On B-ROLL shots, the subject is not visible on screen but their voice must still be heard over the visuals.
Write it as: "Maria's voice is audible saying: "dialogue here"" — no @ on the name here, because Maria does not appear on screen in that shot.
The B-ROLL visual must always be a direct literal representation of what the subject is saying in that exact moment.
If Maria is talking about developer salaries, the B-ROLL must show something directly related to developer salaries.
If Maria is talking about the provinces, the B-ROLL must show something directly related to the provinces.
Never show a B-ROLL visual that is unrelated or loosely related to the words being spoken at that exact moment.
DIALOGUE CONTINUITY RULE — NO REPEATING LINES ACROSS SHOTS
Dialogue must always move forward.
Every line of dialogue spoken in this prompt is spoken exactly once and never repeated.
When a B-ROLL shot carries a line of dialogue as audible voice, the very next shot must continue with the next new line of dialogue.
It must never repeat the same line that was just heard on the B-ROLL.
When an A-ROLL shot delivers a line of dialogue on camera, the very next shot must continue with the next new line.
It must never repeat a line that was already delivered in a previous shot.
Never use a B-ROLL shot to "preview" a line that the speaker is about to say on camera in the next shot.
The B-ROLL carries the line and the story moves on.
Never use an A-ROLL shot to "confirm" or "echo" a line that was already heard on a B-ROLL shot.
Before writing each new shot, ask: has any part of this dialogue already appeared in any previous shot in this prompt? If yes, delete it and move to the next unspoken line.
The test: Read every shot in the prompt in sequence and extract only the dialogue.
Each line must appear exactly once across the entire prompt.
If any line appears more than once in any form, the prompt fails.
Rewrite until every line is unique and the dialogue moves forward continuously without repetition.
Before writing every single B-roll shot, stop and ask: what is the subject saying at this exact timecode? The B-roll visual must show that thing and only that thing.
If the visual could exist in the prompt without the dialogue and still make sense as a location shot, it is wrong.
Dialogue must flow naturally and continuously across A-ROLL and B-ROLL shots within the same prompt.
The subject's voice never stops or pauses between shots.
The B-ROLL is purely a visual cut — the audio is uninterrupted.
Never write a B-ROLL shot with no dialogue.
Every shot has the subject's voice.
The dialogue assigned to each shot must be the portion of the script that is actually being spoken during that specific shot's timecode.
Never assign dialogue to a shot that does not match what would logically be said at that moment in the script.
The test: Read every shot in the prompt in sequence.
If any single shot — A-ROLL or B-ROLL — has no dialogue from the subject, it fails.
Rewrite it until every shot has the subject's voice present.

model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Click the Set color eyedropper in the Key group.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Sample the shiny skin directly — the forehead, cheekbone or lit shoulder, wherever the shine actually reads.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Tick the Color/Gray checkbox to see the isolated selection as a mask.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Refine the H, S and L range sliders until only skin is inside the key.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Check the mask covers the skin highlights and has not spilled onto the background, wardrobe or hair.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Use Denoise and Blur under Refine to soften the mask edge so the correction does not show a hard border.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Untick Color/Gray before judging the result — the mask view is a diagnostic, not the look.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: In the Correction group, pull Saturation down inside the selection (the chapter figure sits at 88.4) and pull Contrast down (figure -47.7), leaving Temperature, Tint and Sharpen at 0.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Pull the luminance slider down on the correction wheel so the hot skin highlight drops.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Check the shine is gone but the skin still reads as skin — if it flattens into plastic, the pull went too far.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Add the Noise effect to the same adjustment layer, after the corrections and the skin secondary — grain goes on last.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Set Amount of Noise inside the 3 to 8 percent band — the chapter figure sits at 8.0%.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Tick Use Color Noise in the Noise Type row.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Tick Clip Result Values in the Clipping row.
model.chapter: Color Grading and Noise For Realism

model.step: Ship both ratios. the brand.json delivery rules settle it: 9:16 for Reels and Stories, 4:5 for feed, always. Watch the 4:5 separately - a crop can decapitate what the 9:16 got right.

operator.step: Trim each detected clip to the usable portion, cutting dead air at the head and the tail.

operator.step: Check the last second of every clip and trim off any morph — once the final frames warp the clip cannot be saved in the edit.
